comments.author: @AtlasAndAgesUS
comments.text: The history section is what I didn't expect — a lounge that started in the 1930s as a private social club with a liquor licence, where the door was literally non-transparent and entry was invitation-only, and then a man being denied entry in Detroit in the late 1960s helped force the door open. That arc, from exclusivity to mass access to overcrowding, makes the ending land harder: the lounges aren't paid for by the $400–$1,000 fees, they're paid for by everyone who swipes a card. Do you think Delta's 3-hour limit and the 18–24 months it says it needs to get on top of overcrowding will actually work, or will the credit card companies just keep adding cardholders faster than the lounges can expand?

That $900 AmEx Platinum card does have a lot of perks. I don't have this card, but I have a friend who does, so I looked into it a bit. If you pay for streaming services and Uber regularly, you'll probably get half your fee back just on those, and then the other perks might get you close to all your money back if used smartly and if those purchases happen to coincide with things you'd be buying anyways.

The "catch" is that it is "only" 1% cash back, when there are some free cards that are 2% back now, so there is some meaningful opportunity cost. But if used strategically, likely for an upper middle income family (or high income family), the AmEx Platinum can be close to free *if* you use it only on things that get you big cash back and also don't use it to justify purchases you wouldn't have otherwise made.
